newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel defends tax plan in hostile upper house.
newsitem.headline: Waigel defends tax plan in hostile upper house.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday defended his tax reform plans in the opposition-controlled upper house of parliament, where key members criticised them as misguided, anti-social and badly financed.

The tax reform plan, which would cut corporate and income tax rates drastically while closing loopholes and broadening the tax base, is expected to pass later this month in parliament's lower house, dominated by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition.
The tax reform is a key part of the government's plan to stimulate investment and jobs growth in an effort to boost the economy, narrow the budget deficit and qualify for European monetary union.

But the upper chamber, comprised of representatives of the mainly Social Democrat (SPD) state governments, is expected to reject the plan in a vote on July 4, opening the way for a mediation committee to take it up on July 10.
The fate of the tax reform could ultimately be tied to a deal on the government's plan to eliminate the corporate capital tax, which is also opposed by the SPD.
The two sides indicated they might soon reach an agreement on the capital tax.
Waigel said international differences in tax systems contributed to Germany's jobs drain as German enterprises expanded in other countries while few foreign companies invest in Germany.
"We must adjust to changes brought by globalisation," Waigel said. "A reform of our tax system is urgently needed to achieve that."

But Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau countered that Waigel's proposed reform would cost the states too much in lost revenues from value added taxes. Social spending must be reformed at the same time, he said.
The SPD says Waigel's plan favours affluent taxpayers, that it would not improve investment conditions and that it would not do enough to stimulate the buying power of lower-income households.
